comments.author: DuskStar
comments.story: The SpaceX Starship is a big deal
comments.why: Explains Curiosity's combined aerobraking, parachute and skycrane landing
comments.text: Curiosity used aerobraking, parachutes AND a skycrane to land. There's a great video here: [VIDEO] Previous solutions weren't used because they were less crazy, but because they were more mass efficient for "small" payload sizes.

comments.author: radiorental
comments.why: Shows JPL simulating, iterating and autogenerating code for complex systems
comments.text: > I still haven't seen any case for visual programming. Aerodef, automotive, etc all use some form of visual programming. Controls engineers rarely write code, the systems are way too complex. E.g. I highly recommend watching this video from JPL to give you an understanding of where such tools excel. It's about simulating, iterating and then having scientists and engineers autogenerate the code they couldn't possibly write or test [VIDEO]

comments.author: layoric
comments.story: NASA's Curiosity rover: 3k days on Mars
comments.why: Illustrates the landing events and Earth-Mars time delay
comments.text: For perceiving the events happening, sure, that was my point. These time differences are nearly always imperceptible but at distances of planets it truly becomes a way of looking into the past. But to be clear, events happen concurrently, eg NASA knew _when_ relative to earth time and _perceived_ events, each stage was "happening" local to Mars vs Earth (assuming it all went well). They made videos about this "7 minutes of terror", I forgot the name of them but linking here [0] [0] [VIDEO]

comments.author: Robotbeat
comments.story: NASA plans to launch a spacecraft to Titan
comments.why: Example of a crazy Mars landing that worked
comments.text: Yup. The robotic program has a very good track record of successes, even for crazy stuff like the Mars Science Laboratory’s sky crane descent stage: [VIDEO] It’s the human spaceflight program that has had the, um, difficulties. There are signs of hope, though.

comments.author: willglynn
comments.story: Hubble Space Telescope Is In Safe Mode After Gyro Failure
comments.why: Curiosity entry, descent and landing sequence used as a comparison
comments.text: There's a video showing the JWST deployment sequence. It's set to calm orchestral music, and the visuals are just 3D renters of the spacecraft. [LINK] This video makes me far more nervous than "7 Minutes of Terror", depicting Curiosity's entry/descent/landing sequence. Far more things have to go right in order for JWST to become operational. [VIDEO]

comments.author: JetDogRush
comments.story: Breaks Observed in Rover Wheel Treads
comments.why: Shows the landing sequence including pyrobolt shock loads
comments.text: Surprisingly the wheels only weigh a few pounds each! (I still can't think in metric and I don't have a real number.) They were primarily constrained by packing volume during cruise ( [LINK] ) and then by shock loads as the securing pyrobolts blew during landing ( [VIDEO] ).
